36.title: The sleeping palace
36.hook: he wakes at night to see the musicians asleep and sprawled; the glamour is gone
36.howItsDone: Buddhists retell the sleeping palace as the night of the great departure, and teachers point to samvega, the jolt of seeing life plainly, as a healthy spur to practice rather than a reason for gloom.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rahula: a son is born, and his name means a fetter. Your line: love, and the fear inside it. Now a new week: the going forth.
screen: `RAHULA — LOVE, AND THE FEAR INSIDE IT.`

segments.voice: Two in the morning, the end of a party. The lights come up and the music stops. The room that looked magical an hour ago is just a room: sticky cups, a torn streamer, someone asleep on the couch with their mouth open. Nothing has changed except the light, and yet everything has. In the story, the prince comes home on the night his son is born, and the palace throws him a celebration: dancers, singers, musicians, all for him. His mind is somewhere else, and he falls asleep in the middle of it. The performers, seeing no one watching, lie down where they are and sleep too. Sometime in the night, the prince wakes up.
screen: `THE LIGHTS COME UP.` → `A PARTY FOR THE PRINCE.` → `HE WAKES IN THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The lamps are still burning, and by their light he sees his palace as it really is. The later telling doesn't spare the details. Dancers sprawled across the floor, instruments dropped beside them. Some snoring, some grinding their teeth, some talking in their sleep, mouths open, clothes in disarray. The people who dazzled him a few hours ago are just tired bodies now. The great hall, the telling says, looked to him like a burial ground. And earlier that evening, one more thing happened. A young woman watching him ride by sang a little verse: happy is the mother, happy the father, happy the wife of a man like this. Her word for happy can also mean cooled, at peace, and it's related to nibbana. The prince heard it and thought: what is it that's truly cooled? And he knew. The fires of wanting, gone out. Put those two moments together and you have today's teaching. The glamour was never in the palace. It was a spell, a way of seeing, and in one night it broke. Buddhists call this feeling samvega: a jolt of clear-eyed urgency, the shock of seeing ordinary life plainly. It isn't disgust with people; the dancers did nothing wrong. It's the moment the prince stops being enchanted and starts being awake to what he'd been looking at all along.

segments.voice: Look around the room you're in as if the lights just came up, and pick one ordinary thing: a chair, a lamp, a pile of laundry, a phone. See it as if for the first time, its shape, its color, what it's for, what it cost, what it will become when it wears out, not to dislike it, just to see it without the story you usually tell about it. Then close your eyes and rest with the breath.

37.title: One look back
37.hook: he looks in on Yasodhara and the baby and does not wake them
37.howItsDone: Buddhists tell the great going forth as the moment of renunciation, and many honor Yasodhara's part in it; the scene is often painted in temple murals, the prince standing at the door of the sleeping room.

segments.voice: Yesterday, samvega: the prince woke to see his glittering hall by plain lamplight. Your line: the spell breaks.

A doorway at night. A child's room, maybe, or a parent's, or someone you loved who was sleeping. You stand there a moment longer than you need to. You don't go in. You don't say anything. You just look. The prince has decided: tonight he will leave the palace, and he has told Channa to saddle his horse. But before he goes, there is one more door he has to stand in. Down the corridor, Yasodhara sleeps, with their newborn son beside her.
screen: `A DOORWAY AT NIGHT.` → `THE DECISION IS MADE.` → `ONE MORE DOOR.`

segments.voice: In the later telling, he opens the door quietly. A lamp is burning. Yasodhara is asleep on a bed strewn with flowers, her hand resting on the baby's head. The prince wants, more than anything, to hold his son. But to lift the child he would have to move her hand, and she would wake. And if she woke, he knew he could not go. So he stays on the threshold. The telling gives him one thought: when I have found what I'm looking for, I will come back and see my son. And he closes the door. It's a tender scene, and one people argue about. Some readers today feel the ache of it: a husband and father walking out at night without a word. Buddhists hold the story in different ways. Some see a great sacrifice, made for the sake of everyone, including this family. Others say plainly that it's hard, and that the story's honesty about the cost matters. The later stories add that Yasodhara, when she learns he has gone to live simply, gives up her own jewels and fine clothes, and that one day both she and Rahula will walk the same path. Whatever you make of the leaving, the scene knows how the hardest goodbyes happen. Not with speeches. In silence, from a doorway, with a hand on the frame. The Pali word for what he's choosing is nekkhamma, renunciation, and the story never pretends it's easy.

38.title: Channa and Kanthaka
38.hook: the charioteer and the white horse ride out at midnight through the city gate
38.howItsDone: Temple murals and carvings across the Buddhist world show the great departure, the prince on the white horse Kanthaka with Channa holding its tail, and some festivals reenact the ride.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nekkhamma: the prince in the doorway, not waking Yasodhara and the baby. Your line: the hardest leaving is quiet.

Who drove you to the airport the first time you really left home? Who sat in the waiting room with you, or carried the boxes up three flights of stairs? Most big journeys have someone at the very start, someone who doesn't come all the way but gets you out the door. The prince has two. It's midnight, and the palace is asleep. In the stable courtyard, his charioteer, Channa, holds the reins of a great white horse named Kanthaka. The prince swings up into the saddle, Channa takes hold of the horse's tail, and the three of them head for the city gate.
screen: `WHO DROVE YOU TO THE AIRPORT?` → `MIDNIGHT IN THE STABLE YARD.` → `THREE HEAD FOR THE GATE.`

segments.voice: The later telling makes this ride glow. Kanthaka is enormous and pure white, and the tradition says both he and Channa were born on the very same day as the prince. No hired driver, no borrowed horse: these are the companions of his whole life. The gods, the telling says, muffled the sound of Kanthaka's hooves with their hands so no one would wake. The city gate, so heavy it took many men to open, swung open by itself. And at the gate a figure appears in the air: Mara, the tempter. Turn back, he says. In seven days you'll be king of the whole world. The prince doesn't even slow down. Mara is patient, and he'll be back in this story. But tonight the three ride on, and by dawn, the telling says, they've crossed three kingdoms. Whatever you make of muffled hooves and opening gates, the heart of the scene is simple and human. The prince did not leave alone. Channa, who answered his questions honestly on the road to the park, now helps him go, knowing it means losing him. Kanthaka carries him as far as a horse can. Every tradition of the story keeps them, and Buddhists remember them with real affection. Great journeys are often told as solo adventures. This one, the most famous departure in Buddhism, begins with a friend holding a horse's tail in the dark.

39.title: The cut hair
39.hook: at the river Anoma he cuts his hair with his sword and puts on a simple robe
39.howItsDone: In Theravada novice ordination, called pabbajja, the head is shaved and a robe put on; in Myanmar, boys going through shinbyu are dressed as princes before being robed as novices for a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kanthaka: the white horse, with Channa alongside, who carried the prince out at midnight. Your line: someone rode with you.

By dawn, the three riders reach a river. The later telling names it the Anoma. The prince gets down from Kanthaka on the sandy bank, still dressed as what he was: a prince in silk and jewels, his long hair bound up in a royal topknot. People sometimes cut their hair after something ends, a breakup, a new job, a hard year, and the mirror shows someone lighter, someone starting over. Hair can carry who we've been. The prince draws his sword. Channa watches.
screen: `DAWN AT THE RIVER.` → `HAIR IS WHO WE'VE BEEN.` → `HE DRAWS HIS SWORD.`

segments.voice: He takes his long hair in one hand and cuts through it with the sword. In the telling, what's left is short, curling to the right, and it stays that length for the rest of his life; tradition links this to the small tight curls on statues of the Buddha. He throws the topknot into the air. He takes off his royal clothes, puts on a simple robe the color of earth, like the wanderer from the fourth sight, and gives his jewels to Channa to take home. In that moment, the prince is gone. There's a samana on the riverbank. The word for this is pabbajja, going forth: leaving the household life for the homeless one. It's still the word for it. In Theravada communities, when someone becomes a novice monk or nun, the ceremony is called pabbajja, and the head is shaved, as on that riverbank. In Myanmar, there's a ceremony for boys called shinbyu: first they're dressed up as princes, in silk and makeup, and paraded through town, then their heads are shaved and they put on robes for a time, retelling this very morning with their own lives. What pabbajja teaches, even for people who never shave a head, is that some things we carry are costumes. The prince didn't hate his hair or his jewels. He just didn't need them for where he was going. There was simply less to carry.

40.title: Do you have to leave?
40.hook: the prince left home; most Buddhists never have. An old couple asks the Buddha how to stay together, in this life and the next (AN 4.55)
40.howItsDone: Most Buddhists are lay followers who practice at home, keeping the five precepts, giving, and visiting the temple on holy days, while monks and nuns live the renunciant life the prince chose.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pabbajja, going forth: the cut hair, and the plain robe. Your line was less to carry. Day forty.

On the riverbank, the prince sends Channa home with the white horse. In the later telling, Kanthaka's heart breaks on the road, and he dies of grief. Back at the palace, a wife and a newborn son wake up to an empty room. It's the part of the story many people find hardest. And it raises a question a lot of newcomers carry quietly: if this is the path, do I have to leave the people I love? Today, the answer the old texts give, through a married couple.
screen: `KANTHAKA'S HEART BREAKS.` → `AN EMPTY ROOM AT THE PALACE.` → `DO I HAVE TO LEAVE?`

segments.voice: Start with who was there. The early texts describe the Buddha's community as four groups: monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen. The lay followers are called upasaka and upasika. They farmed, traded, married, raised children, and most Buddhists in history have lived that way. Now the couple. In a town called Sumsumaragira lived an old householder known as Nakula's father, and his wife, Nakula's mother. One day he tells the Buddha: since she was brought to my home as a young girl, I don't remember being unfaithful to her, not even in thought. We want to see each other in this life, and in the next one too. She says the same. The Buddha doesn't tell them to let each other go. He tells them how: if a husband and wife both wish to stay together, in this life and the next, let them be matched in four things, faith, virtue, generosity and wisdom. Later he named the two of them foremost among his lay followers in trust. So what is the letting go that the teaching asks for? Teachers draw a line between love and the grip. Love wishes someone well. The grip needs them never to change, never to leave, never to be anything but yours. That grip is where so much fear lives, and that's what the practice loosens. Monks and nuns choose a different life, and the tradition honors them. But for most people on this path, the practice happens at a kitchen table, with the people they love.

41.title: The king's offer
41.hook: in Rajagaha King Bimbisara offers him wealth; he declines (Sn 3.1), and later tradition adds his promise to return if he finds the way
41.howItsDone: Buddhists remember King Bimbisara as one of the Buddha's great lay supporters, and the Pabbajja Sutta, the poem of this meeting, is still recited and studied as an early account of the going forth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, upasaka: most Buddhists practice at home, and an old couple asked the Buddha how to stay together. Your line: love without the grip.

Rajagaha, capital of the kingdom of Magadha. A stranger with a shaved head walks from house to house with a bowl, eyes lowered, taking whatever is put in it. From his palace, King Bimbisara sees him, and something in the way this man walks makes the king send messengers after him. Turning down something bad is easy. Turning down something good, more money, a promotion, a place in someone's big plans, is a different kind of hard. That's what's coming on a hillside outside the city.
screen: `A STRANGER WITH A BOWL.` → `THE KING WATCHES FROM ABOVE.` → `SAYING NO TO SOMETHING GOOD.`

segments.voice: This scene is in the Pali canon itself, in a poem in the Sutta Nipata called the Going Forth. The king sees that this beggar is no ordinary beggar. He walks mindfully, the poem says, eyes down, looking only a yoke's length ahead. The messengers find him on a hill outside the city, eating his alms food, and the king comes out in his chariot to meet him. Then the offer. You're young, you're clearly of noble birth. Come and lead my army. Take wealth, and enjoy it. The wanderer answers calmly. He tells the king where he comes from: a people of the Himalayan foothills, the Sakyans. He didn't leave home looking for pleasures, he says. He's seen the danger in them, and he sees safety in letting them go. I'm going to strive. That's where my heart is. The poem ends there. The later commentaries add one more exchange, and it's the one people remember. The king says: then when you find what you're looking for, come back here first and teach me. And the wanderer promises he will. Tradition says he kept that promise, and the story will get there. What the scene shows is a no that isn't rude, bitter or proud. He declines a kingdom, kindly, and leaves the door open. A promise to come back says: this no isn't about you. It's about the road.

42.title: Two teachers
42.hook: he masters the deep states taught by Alara Kalama and Uddaka Ramaputta, and leaves: good, but not the end (MN 26)
42.howItsDone: Buddhist meditators still study the deep absorptions and formless states, and teachers often tell the story of the two teachers to show that calm states, however deep, are a means rather than the goal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bimbisara offered wealth and an army, and the wanderer said no, kindly. Your line: a promise to come back. Today, the last day of the going forth.

What comes after getting good at something? Years on a language, an instrument, a craft, and people start coming to you for advice. Then, right at the top of it, a quiet question can show up anyway: is this it? Not because the thing is bad. Because it isn't what you came for. The wanderer left the palace to find an answer to age, sickness and death, and in his world there are teachers of meditation with communities of students around them. He goes to the first.
screen: `GOOD AT SOMETHING.` → `IS THIS IT?` → `A TEACHER WITH A COMMUNITY.`

segments.voice: This story comes from the Buddha himself, in a sutta where he looks back on his search. His first teacher was Alara Kalama, who taught a meditation leading to a very deep state called the base of nothingness: a mind so still it rests in nothing at all. The wanderer learned it fast, and soon could reach it himself. Alara was delighted, and did something generous. You know what I know, he said. Let's lead this community together, as equals. The wanderer thought about it and said no. This teaching, he says, doesn't lead to the end of suffering, only to that state. When you come out of it, you're still you, with everything you carried in. So he went to a second teacher, Uddaka Ramaputta, whose father had taught an even subtler state: neither perception nor non-perception, a stillness so fine it can barely be described. Again he mastered it. Again he was offered leadership, this time of the whole community. Again he said no, and walked away. Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't call these teachers frauds or these states useless. Buddhists still teach these deep meditative states today, and later suttas list them among the attainments of meditation. What he says is simpler: good, but not the end. That's this week, the going forth, in one line: samvega, the doorway, the midnight ride, the cut hair, a horse's grief, Bimbisara's offer, and two teachers. Each time, something good is left behind, because it isn't the end.
screen: `ALARA — THE BASE OF NOTHINGNESS.` · `LET'S LEAD TOGETHER. NO.` · `UDDAKA — SUBTLER STILL. NO.` · `NOT FRAUDS. JUST NOT THE END.` · then, large: `GOOD, BUT NOT THE END.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you've learned well, a skill, a subject, a habit, a practice, and give it its due for a breath or two: the hours it took, the work it was. Then ask it gently, what's next, not to throw it away, just to see if there's a further step, a deeper question, something it points toward. Let the question sit beside the skill without rushing for an answer.
Two teachers. Alara Kalama and Uddaka Ramaputta, who taught the wanderer deep meditative states, and whom he left because the states were good, but not the end.
Your line: good, but not the end. Two masters, two kind offers, two quiet refusals. A week of leaving, finished.

original.note: Pali: the base of nothingness, the deep state Alara Kalama taught.

trapdoor: what you thought: the wanderer took a couple of meditation classes.
what it means: he mastered the deepest states his two teachers taught, and left, because they were good, but not the end.
what a scholar hears: MN 26 (Ariyapariyesana Sutta): Alara taught the base of nothingness, Uddaka (through his father Rama) the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; neither led to nibbana.
